extracted.intended_audience: aspiring sitcom/TV comedy writers and fans who want to learn writers' room lingo
extracted.subtask_description: A glossary-style guide to common sitcom writers' room terms and comedic devices used in television scriptwriting, with brief definitions and usage notes. Useful for writers, showrunners, and anyone who wants to 'talk like a real sitcom writer.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Callbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing a joke based on something already mentioned in the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use callbacks to reward attentive viewers and build running jokes; place them where they reference earlier material for comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hey May
rubrics_metrics.description: Supposedly from Carl Reiner and the old DICK VAN DYKE SHOW. It’s an act break so great that a husband yells to his wife in the kitchen: 'Hey, May, you gotta get in here!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refers to an exceptionally strong act break that compels audience attention; modeled on classic TV timing and surprise before commercial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swinging in on a rope
rubrics_metrics.description: A side character enters the screen, delivers a joke, then leaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to punctuate a scene with a quick laugh (example: Carla on CHEERS). Effective for punchy, transient character jokes that don't require scene time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Button
rubrics_metrics.description: Final joke of a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scene-closing laugh or gag; should land cleanly and often set up the next scene or act break. Critics may question whether an ending line qualifies as a true 'button.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow
rubrics_metrics.description: Same as button but sounds more 'street'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interchangeable with 'button' in function; choice of term reflects room culture/tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipe
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition. (Example: a character whose basic function is to come into the room and deliver pipe; e.g., a character named Piper.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label for lines or characters that primarily deliver background information; avoid heavy-handed pipe that stalls natural dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clam
rubrics_metrics.description: Overused joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flags material that has become stale in the room; watch for repetition and avoid landing on a gag that's already been exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheboygan
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke too over-the-top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used dismissively to describe jokes that go beyond plausibility or tonal fit; cultural/room-specific term—usage varies by writers' rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: B story
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot. Often used to give cast members not involved in the main story something to do and keep them off the writers' backs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can provide comic variety and ensemble use; debated among writers—some avoid B-stories (e.g., 'No B-stories...ever' rule) while others find them often funnier or more memorable than the A-story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that occur in a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small units of action or story rhythm; structure scenes by beats to control pacing and comedic timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: House number
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitching an idea or joke that’s more of an example than the actual pitch you intend to go in the script; a prefatory example used as a disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a house number to test an idea without committing; it's a way to present a proof-of-concept in the pitch, but be aware it may be mistaken for the actual intended pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savers
rubrics_metrics.description: Damage control jokes right after your real joke pitch dies a horrible death. It was Johnny Carson's best friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare quick fallback jokes to rescue a failed pitch or live moment; scripted savers can be used intentionally or reactively to regain audience laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captain Obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointing out a problem that even the craft services guy could identify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pejorative for stating the obvious in dialogue; avoid characters merely narrating facts the audience already understands unless done intentionally for comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar police
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers whose only contribution in rewrites is correcting grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tongue-in-cheek label for contributors who focus on surface issues rather than story; use diplomacy when handling such notes to avoid derailing substantive rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofer’s Challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Some technicality you come across during a rewrite that’s not worth everyone’s time to settle (e.g., what food should be on the table? what was the year of that Superbowl?). It's left to the person proofing that night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defer trivial continuity or factual details to the proofer to avoid bogging down table reads; reserve writers' room time for bigger story problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Throwing a bone
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving an actor a joke because he doesn’t have much to do in a scene or you don’t think he’s very good but have to service him anyway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often a political or practical compromise to placate actors or network notes; be mindful that such concessions can affect story quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coconut drop
rubrics_metrics.description: (NewsRadio room term) When a character suddenly behaves in an uncharacteristic way for a specific reason (e.g., Gilligan suddenly being smart because of a coconut falling on him).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes contrived, situational devices used to force a plot point or gag; avoid over-reliance as it can feel like a cheat.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Here we are in sunny Spain"
rubrics_metrics.description: Danny Arnold's contemptuous phrase for exposition he considered too bald—when one character tells another something they both already know (but the audience doesn't).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flags awkward expository dialogue; rewrite to make exposition sound more natural and integrated into character action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hang a lantern on it
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with a completely impossible situation that nonetheless has to be happening and can't be explained, writers 'hang a lantern on it'—note the anomaly and move on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tactic to acknowledge implausible plot elements briefly rather than laboring over a technical explanation; often used in genre shows where strict realism isn't required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nokimura
rubrics_metrics.description: When you're so sure a funny name is going to get laughs you weave it through the entire script and it dies every single time; the table will reject it thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against overusing a gimmicky running-name joke; if a name-based gag fails in the room, don't persist with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act break (practical definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An act break is typically the moment immediately before a commercial when something surprising/funny happens to leave the audience hooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good act break should create tension or a strong laugh that encourages viewers to return after commercials; classic examples can inspire similar beats ('Hey May').
